theme: Blood; sexual purity; love your neighbor
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 17:1-19:37. This reading includes the unit’s anchor verse in chapter 17 and the well-known command to love your neighbor in chapter 19. Look for the connection between the sacrificial laws and the everyday ethical commands.
settingTheScene: With the Day of Atonement behind them, the book of Leviticus turns from how a holy God is approached to how a holy people live. Chapters 17 to 26 are often called the Holiness Code, because the refrain “You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (19:2) runs through them. Chapter 17 gives the reason for the prohibition on eating blood. Chapter 18 sets out sexual boundaries in contrast to Egypt and Canaan. Chapter 19 gathers a wide variety of commands for ordinary life.
observation: All sacrifices must be brought to the tent of meeting, and not offered in the open field (17:1-9).
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls, for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life” (17:11).
The prohibition of eating blood applies to sojourners too (17:10-14).
Israel is not to live as Egypt or Canaan do (18:3).
The laws of sexual conduct in chapter 18 are given because the nations around them “defiled” the land (18:24-30).
“You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy” (19:2).
The commands in chapter 19 include leaving the edges of the field for the poor (19:9-10), not stealing or lying (19:11), not withholding wages (19:13), and showing impartiality (19:15).
“You shall love your neighbor as yourself: I am the LORD” (19:18). “The stranger who sojourns with you shall be to you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself” (19:34).
interpretation:
Leviticus 17:11 is the key to the whole sacrificial system, and it is the anchor verse of this unit. It tells you why blood is used. It is not because blood is magical. It is because “the life of the flesh is in the blood.” Blood represents life, and life is given on the altar in the place of the sinner’s life. “I have given it for you.” The sacrifice is not a human invention to placate an angry God. It is something God himself provided. He gave the blood on the altar for your atonement. The system is a gift.

It also teaches that atonement is costly. A life is given. Sin is not forgiven cheaply. This is not a cruel principle. It reflects how seriously God takes sin, and how seriously he takes the value of life.

The chapters that follow show what holy people look like. Notice that the same chapter that commands “You shall be holy” also commands leaving the edge of your field for the poor and paying a worker his wages at the end of each day. Holiness is not only about worship. It is about how you treat your neighbor, your employee, the deaf person, the blind person, and the foreigner. “You shall not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind” (19:14) is one of the sharpest examples. The vulnerable are protected because God is watching, and “I am the LORD” is repeated like a signature on each command.

The great command in verse 18, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” is in the middle of this chapter. It is not a new idea in the New Testament. It is the center of the law. The love is practical: it shows itself in honesty, fairness, and generosity. And verse 34 extends it to the foreigner, with a reminder: “for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.” The memory of their own redemption is the basis for how they treat others.

The chapters also remind us that the call to holiness comes after atonement. The people can be holy because their sins have been covered. Grace comes first, and the life of holiness follows.
connection: Jesus calls the command to love your neighbor the second greatest in the law (Matthew 22:39), and he explains it in the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37). Paul says that “the whole law is fulfilled in one word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Galatians 5:14). Peter quotes Leviticus 19:2 in 1 Peter 1:15-16. And Hebrews 9:22 says, “Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins,” based on Leviticus 17:11. Christ is the one whose blood was given for us.
application:
Read Leviticus 17:11 several times. Consider what it means that God gave the blood for you.

Choose one command from chapter 19 that speaks to your life. Where could you practice it this week?

Think of someone in your community who is a stranger or an outsider. How could you show love to them?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the life given for you.
Ask him to make you holy as he is holy.
Ask him to teach you to love your neighbor and the stranger.
